ENT Clinical Note – Tele-consultation  

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure  
  – New shortness of breath / chest tightness beginning 2–3 days ago while running with a friend.  
• Symptom timeline and progression  
  – Day 0: First noted dyspnoea on exertion; previously able to converse while running.  
  – Day 1-3: Dyspnoea now with brisk walking; persistent wheeze and dry cough.  
  – Salbutamol (“blue inhaler”) used repeatedly with minimal relief.  
• ENT-relevant symptoms  
  – Throat swelling/closure sensation: none reported.  
  – Voice change/hoarseness: none.  
  – Dysphagia/odynophagia/drooling: none.  
  – Nasal/ocular: chronic seasonal hay-fever only; no acute coryza.  
  – Stridor/noisy breathing: expiratory wheeze only (patient-reported).  
  – Dyspnea: present as described above.  
  – Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling: none.  
  – Ear/neck symptoms: none.  
• Relevant past episodes and treatments  
  – Last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; never hospitalized; no prior oral steroids or antibiotics.  
  – No prior ED visits for asthma.  
• Allergies and current medications  
  – Allergies: seasonal hay-fever; denies medication allergies.  
  – Current meds:  
    • Salbutamol MDI 100 µg/actuation, dose/freq: PRN (currently several times daily; not documented).  
    • Clenil (beclomethasone) inhaler 100 µg, 3 puffs BID.  
    • Cetraben emollient (topical) – dose/freq not documented.  
    • Hydrocortisone 1% topical cream – PRN for presumed eczema.  
    • No rescue epinephrine device.  
• Social context  
  – Physically active runner; lives at home (address confirmed). No supervision issues stated.

Objective:
• Observable swelling: none reported.  
• Airway/breathing: patient reports wheeze; no stridor.  
• Mental status: normal conversational.  
• Vitals and physical examination: Not recorded (tele-consult; no peak-flow performed).  
• Accompaniment: not specified; patient alone during call.

Assessment:
• Working impression: Mild-to-moderate asthma exacerbation (loss of prior control), likely exercise- and/or allergen-triggered.  
  – Evidence: known asthma, 2–3-day increase in wheeze/cough/SOB, inadequate response to reliever, preventer under-dosed, no infection or systemic features.  
• Differential diagnosis (from DDx, aligned with transcript)  
  1. Viral URTI–triggered asthma flare – possible; abrupt onset, cough; no fever (opposing: no upper-respiratory symptoms).  
  2. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction / poor inhaler technique – contributes; symptoms began during running; now persist beyond exercise (opposing: now symptomatic at rest).  
  – Other DDx such as pulmonary embolism or pneumonia considered low likelihood; no supporting features.  

Plan:
• Pharmacologic adjustments (agreed during consult)  
  – Increase Clenil to 4 puffs BID until reviewed.  
  – Continue Salbutamol up to every 2 hours PRN; if requiring this frequency, consider urgent care.  
• Monitoring / escalation instructions  
  – If breathing worsens, speech becomes difficult, peak-flow drops (if measured), or relief <3 h after Salbutamol → attend A&E immediately or call EMS (999).  
• Follow-up  
  – Book face-to-face GP appointment within next few days for chest exam, peak-flow assessment, and review of inhaler technique; consider oral steroids and/or antibiotics depending on findings.  
  – Arrange formal asthma review (nurse-led) since last review was >2 years ago.  
• Education / prevention  
  – Reinforce correct inhaler technique and adherence to preventer.  
  – Advise avoidance of known triggers (pollen, intense exercise during acute flare).  
  – Discuss obtaining home peak-flow meter and recording diary (to be done at review).  

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements  
  – No objective vitals, oxygen saturation, or peak-flow recorded.  
  – Inhaler technique not demonstrated.  
  – Formal drug allergy list incomplete beyond “none.”  
  – No documentation of smoking status, occupational exposures, or COVID-19 vaccine status.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx  
  – Medication name misheard (“Flanel/Bactroban”) vs. “Clenil” beclomethasone – resolved to Clenil; conflict noted but clinically immaterial.  
● Transcript quality  
  – Generally clear; occasional audio overlap and mis-heard medication names.
